terms.comment: Its first sense is “lent, borrowed”: pecūniās mūtuās sūmere, to borrow money (Cic. Phil. 10.26); then, given and returned, on both sides.

evidence: Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10.15.4: mē mūtuō dīligās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “The same back”: mūtuō mehercule, “and we feel the same, truly”. With a verb, inter sē often does the work (see each other).

phrases.latin: paulisper alter alterīus cōnspectū, admīrātiōne mūtuā prope attonitī, conticuēre
phrases.english: for a little while, each at the sight of the other, almost stunned with mutual admiration, they fell silent

phrases.latin: cupis post longum tempus neptem tuam mēque ūnā vidēre. grātum est utrīque nostrum quod cupis, mūtuō mehercule
phrases.english: you long to see your granddaughter, and me with her, after so long. We are both glad that you do, and truly, the feeling is mutual

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-livius, loci-plinius), checked there against the editions they name.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 349.
